AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: An ectopic pregnancy after hysterectomy is a rare but potentially life-threatening event. Women with this condition might not be appropriately investigated, resulting in delays in diagnosis and treatment.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To characterize cases of ectopic pregnancy occurring after hysterectomy.

AbstractText.Label: SEARCH STRATEGY
AbstractText.content: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched using the terms "pregnancy, abdominal" or "pregnancy, tubal" or "pregnancy, ectopic" and "hysterectomy" or "post-hysterectomy" or "post hysterectomy."

AbstractText.Label: SELECTION CRITERIA
AbstractText.content: Case reports or case series published in English up to October 10, 2016, were included. Cases were included if the diagnosis was confirmed by definitive tests such as serum or urine β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) testing, ultrasonography evidence of pregnancy, or histology.

AbstractText.Label: DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS
AbstractText.content: Case characteristics were extracted via a standard spreadsheet.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN RESULTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 57 cases were included in the analysis. Abdominal pain was the predominant symptom. Implantation in a remaining fallopian tube was common. Most patients were managed surgically.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: A high index of suspicion and a low threshold for performing a β-hCG pregnancy test is recommended in all women presenting with clinical symptoms of ectopic pregnancy, regardless of the hysterectomy status. This could lead to earlier diagnosis and fewer complications. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
